Il ferro accorcia il T2*: nelle sequenze: Iron shortens T2*: in multi-echo gradient-echo sequences the signal of iron-loaded tissue falls faster the more iron there is. You draw an ROI and fit a curve S(TE) = S0·e^(−TE/T2*); R2* = 1000/T2* (s⁻¹). Heart: full-thickness ROI on the interventricular septum of the mid-ventricular short-axis slice (away from the susceptibility artifacts of the cardiac veins and lung in the lateral wall). Cardiac thresholds at 1.5 T: T2* > 20 ms normal, 10-20 ms mild-moderate overload, < 10 ms severe. Liver: ROI in the right-lobe parenchyma away from vessels; the liver iron concentration (LIC, mg Fe/g dry weight) is estimated from R2* with a calibration curve (the collection uses Garbowski 2014: LIC ≈ 0.029·R2*^1.014). Most used LIC classes: < 2 mg/g normal (up to about 1.8), 2-7 mild, 7-15 moderate, > 15 severe. With very low signal, noise creates a «floor»: a fit on all echoes overestimates T2*; truncation of the late echoes or a model with a constant (offset) is used. In the viewer, the T2* tool (More measurements → T2*) copies the ROI to all echoes of the slice, shows the curve, T2* and R2* with both models and, for the liver, the LIC. Here ferritin is relatively low (1,191 µg/L), but MRI shows a liver that is almost black from the second-third echo (T2* 1.6 ms, LIC 19.9 mg/g: severe) and a septum that darkens more than muscle (T2* 11 ms: mild-moderate, close to the severe threshold). The spleen also loses signal rapidly: in transfusional overload iron accumulates in the macrophages of the reticuloendothelial system (liver and spleen), whereas in primary hemochromatosis the spleen is spared. Ferritin is an indirect and imperfect marker: it does not replace the measurement of iron in the heart and liver.
